title: A Japanese name list built from the Indus sign pictures scores +186 on the viral AI decipherment's contest, close to the paper's Tamil +223
body: Deliberately and in the open, we built a list of real Japanese names of every kind that contain words for the pictured things on the signs. With the paper's code unchanged it scores +186, and on seals held out from every choice it ties the paper's Tamil list (+105 against +104). Picking Japanese names by score, tested on unseen seals, also reaches Tamil's level. Picture words alone do not do it; the mix of place, mountain and shrine names does. Each check was fixed in advance. A score that list-building moves this far cannot identify the seals' language.

title: Two rebuilt Old Tamil lists score +4 and +49 on the viral AI decipherment's contest, against the paper's +223
body: We had a fresh AI agent build a second list of Old Tamil names from the same kinds of sources as the paper, and ran the paper's code unchanged. It scores +4, about the same as scrambled names. A third list, built with the paper's prompt unchanged except for language and sources, scores +49. Checks fixed in advance show the gap is not the picture words and not the honorific endings: it is which names are in the list (the paper's names the second list lacks score +218; the second list's own names −96). Tamil's sister languages are weak tests: Old Telugu and Old Kannada are void (the method reads under three signs once Sanskrit loans are dropped), and Old Malayalam does not beat its control. An independent review found a change we had made to the name-builder prompt; we logged it and tested it. The new interactive chart in the article shows every run.

title: Three more languages on the viral AI decipherment's contest: Tamil stays top, but beating chance is not special
body: We ran the paper's code, unchanged, on Sumerian, Egyptian and Finnish names, with rules fixed in advance. No new language reaches half of Tamil's score (Sumerian comes closest: +104 against +223). But every language with real names except Sanskrit beats its scrambled control in most runs (Finnish in 10 of 10), so beating chance is what real names do on these seals, whatever the language. By our preregistered rule the panel verdict is mixed.

title: The viral AI 'decipherment' beats noise, not the placebo that matters
body: A paper going viral says AI read the Indus script as early Tamil (Raj 2026). We ran its own code on its own data. It reproduces exactly, and it beats scrambled names and fake seals. But it fails the test that matters: move Tamil's picture words onto the wrong signs and Tamil scores the same (223 against 224, p = 0.51). 59% of its readings are words that only sound like the picture. Japanese family names, a language with no known link to the Indus, score 60% as well as Tamil and beat it in 4 of 10 runs, though they just miss the bar we set in advance (7 of 10 runs, 8 needed). Its copper-tablet 'proof' counts copies: counted once per distinct text, p = 0.19. The author published everything, which is why we could check it in a day. A fluent reading is not a decipherment; that takes a test that can fail, fixed in advance. Our preprint: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24579269.

title: Our refutations mostly survive other sign lists
body: We had checked our positive findings under 12 other ways of dividing the signs and under the second edition of the texts, but never our refutations. Now we have. Four of the six hold everywhere they can be tested, including the 'tablets are licences' and 'animal emblems name organisations' readings. Two cannot be checked this way: the stroked-jar result rests on one edition, and the cup-fee result has only one alternative test, which shows a drift over time that was already known. On a fresh look, three blind raters moved the claim by Laursen and Parpola that 'Gulf seals write another language' from refuted to untestable: our test ruled out only a stricter version of the claim.

title: Testing our own test on a script we can read
body: Before trusting our meaning tests on Indus, we ran one of them on Linear B, cut to Indus size. One agent who reads Linear B wrote 30 true claims, another invented 30 claims without being able to read it. The test never passed an invented claim and never rejected a true one, but it gave no answer on 27 of the 30 true claims. So a pass means something, but it confirms a sign pair, not a reading. With that in view, two blind raters moved Parpola's 'names of the god Murukan' from supported to untestable: the sign pair is real, but it fits other readings just as well.

title: Jar signs with strokes are not volume units on pots
body: Mukhopadhyay read jar signs with one to three strokes inside as units of volume. If so, they should turn up more often on pottery. Two agents, working blind, matched her drawings to the standard sign numbers and agreed. The signs appear on fewer pots than chance predicts (17 against 23 expected), in a test that would have seen a twofold excess. Parpola's fig + fish 'north star' could not be tested: his fig sign has no number we can check, and the two agents disagreed on it.

title: The SIGIL emblem model can't be tested at Indus size
body: SIGIL claims a system of emblems with no sounds can produce the Indus patterns. We fitted it to texts and checked it on data held back. Run first on texts SIGIL itself produced, the check rejected 98 of 100, so it can't tell SIGIL from a poor fit. The Indus held-out texts were left unread. On the scorecard SIGIL moves from pending to untestable.

title: Numbers on tablets are fixed, not counts
body: If Indus tablets were tallies of goods, their numerals should vary more than those on seals. A Latin check showed the test can see such a gap at Indus sizes. Instead, numbers on tablets vary less than on seals at both Harappa and Mohenjo-daro; they come in fixed pairs such as 3 + one sign, as in names.

title: Scorecard: every Indus claim on one scale
body: Two raters, working blind under rules fixed in advance, placed 65 claims (sound keys, 44 meaning claims and our own findings) on one scale; they agreed well (kappa 0.84). None is anchored or has predicted new data. Eleven survive a test that could have refuted them, seven are refuted, and the rest can't be tested yet or can't be checked at all.

title: Tablets quoting seals can't be seen at Indus size
body: Before testing whether Indus tablets repeat sign runs from seals of their own city, we ran the same test on real Ur III seals and tablets cut to Indus size. It caught the real link in only 31% of trials, so the Indus test was not run.

title: Test sealed for any Meluhha seal photos that arrive
body: We asked the Nisaba archive, CDLI and Yale for photos of tablets that may carry Indus or Gulf seal impressions. How we will score any photo is fixed in advance; one seal pattern turns up on 3 of 17 foreign finds, so a match on it alone would be weak.

title: Neighbouring scripts offer no new route on open data
body: We read recent work on Linear Elamite, Proto-Elamite, Cypro-Minoan, Linear A, Rongorongo and machine decipherment. Each advance used something already known that touches the texts, such as names read in cuneiform; for Indus no such anchor is open.

title: Image search for foreign seals on clay tablets closed
body: The one known Gulf seal impression, on Yale tablet YBC 5447, looks like a rolled cylinder band on the museum photo. A trained detector, a zero-shot test and a blind visual review all missed it, so spotting these seals needs an expert eye, not a shape search.

title: Stamp detector failed its sealed gate
body: On Yale's open tablet photos the detector found 44% of known stamp impressions and none of the 5 controls, below the bar we set before running it. We did not run the full sweep.

title: Seal texts barely differ between cities
body: Readable seal and label corpora from Mesopotamia and Roman provinces can be told apart by site (AUC 0.66 to 0.88). Mohenjo-daro and Harappa seals score 0.49, no better than chance, so we find no large city-specific stock of signs.

title: Ten AI guessers agreeing does not make a guess right
body: Rehearsed on proto-cuneiform signs with known meanings, guesses that most of ten blind guessers agreed on were right only 1 time in 4. Agreement came from shared errors, so we will not use it on Indus signs.

title: Search-size result softened to mixed
body: A check on three Latin test cells came out one solved, one limited by the search and one limited by the scoring. We changed the claim in the README and the findings to say the evidence is mixed.

title: Seal carvers and texts: not confirmed
body: A sealed test linking carving hands to text content passed narrowly (p = 0.0098 against a bar of 0.01), but two reruns gave 0.0105 and 0.017, and text length may explain it. We record it as not confirmed.

title: Plan redone from scratch
body: A fresh agent planned the decipherment without reading our repo. It put the 2027 odds near 1% and found one untried route, a search for Indus seal impressions on Mesopotamian tablets, which we then tested.
